claims.text: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles can comprise five or more metals.
HEA nanoparticles can be immobilized on supports such as Al2O3.
The degree of homogeneous elemental mixing at the surface primarily governs HEA nanoparticle premelting and melting behavior.
A random, homogeneous elemental distribution produces diverse local bonding environments and local lattice distortions.
The surface distribution of alloying elements produces surface-energy heterogeneity.
Local lattice distortions and surface-energy variations increase the energy barrier for surface-atom diffusion.
Elemental segregation creates surface regions with statistically weaker bonding.
Weakly bonded segregated regions permit easier atomic mobility and cause earlier, more progressive premelting.
Homogeneously mixed HEA nanoparticles will have a higher premelting-onset temperature than segregated counterparts.
Homogeneously mixed HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a sharper melting transition, whereas segregated particles will melt more gradually.
Uniformly mixed particles will maintain surface integrity to a higher fraction of the bulk melting temperature than segregated particles.
The proposed relationship should hold typically for HEA nanoparticles 5–10 nm in size.
The proposed relationship should hold up to approximately 0.6–0.7 times the melting temperature.
Premelting-onset differences may vary with HEA composition, synthesis method, and support interaction.
Particle-size distribution may affect the observed premelting and melting behavior.
Differential scanning calorimetry can determine the onset temperature of nanoparticle premelting in the proposed experiment.
In-situ TEM imaging can monitor surface-atom mobility during the proposed heating experiment.
Supported HEA nanoparticles are promising for catalysis and chemical sensing.
Multicomponent nanoparticles of the type considered are relevant to energy-storage applications.
High-entropy alloys can exhibit thermal stability.
